title: Elon Musk confirms discussions with TSMC about Terafab chipmaking collaboration — Intel is the only other named partner, Terafab to exclusively supply Tesla, SpaceX, and xAI
source_used: Tom's Hardware (citing Tim Culpan's Culpium newsletter)
key_facts: Tim Culpan's Culpium newsletter reported on Friday 2 Oct 2026 that TSMC and Musk's Terafab chip project are discussing a collaboration in which TSMC would build and operate a fab serving only Tesla, SpaceX and xAI.
Musk confirmed the talks on X early Saturday 3 Oct 2026 without detail; TSMC has not commented.

Culpan's most likely structure: TSMC owns and operates the fab, SpaceX/Terafab invests and/or commits to guaranteed chip volumes; an alternative gives SpaceX majority ownership with TSMC operating and supplying process technology.
Culpium links TSMC's rumoured Texas fab complex plans to supporting Terafab.
Intel is so far the only named Terafab partner, due to supply its 14A (1.4nm-class) process; Tom's Hardware says TSMC involvement could push Intel's 14A out.
Tom's Hardware notes a patent angle: Intel has a cross-licence with TSMC but Terafab does not, so chips made on an Intel node could raise TSMC patent issues.
Nothing is official; Tom's Hardware calls both structures speculation.
quote_evidence: "Just discussions, but something may come of it," Musk wrote in an X post, while TSMC has so far remained tight-lipped.
For now, Intel is to supply its 1.4nm-class 14A process technology to Terafab, which would produce chips for Elon Musk's SpaceX, Tesla, and xAI.
Since nothing is official at this point, both 'Plan A' and 'Plan B' should be considered as speculations rather than the two options currently on the table
why_it_matters_hint: A TSMC-run fab dedicated to Musk's companies would reshape Terafab and could squeeze out Intel's role as its process supplier.
event_date: 2-3 Oct 2026 (Culpium report Friday 2 Oct, Musk confirmation Saturday 3 Oct)
notes: Chain: Culpium first reported the talks; Tom's Hardware added Musk's X confirmation and its own analysis. Treated as 'Tom's Hardware reports, citing Culpium'. Ownership structures are the newsletter's analysis, not confirmed.
